title: What is DA-CAR
content: DA-CAR is the Cordillera Administrative Region office of the Department of Agriculture. It implements DA programs in Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Kalinga, Mountain Province, and Baguio City, supporting farmers and fishers with extension services, inputs, equipment, and market linkages.
keywords: DA-CAR; regional office; Cordillera; extension services

title: Agencies related to DA-CAR
content: Common partner agencies include the Bureau of Plant Industry (BPI), Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI), Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), Philippine Rice Research Institute (PhilRice), Philippine Carabao Center (PCC), Agricultural Training Institute (ATI), Philippine Crop Insurance Corporation (PCIC), and the Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority (FPA).
agency: DA; BPI; BAI; BFAR; PhilRice; PCC; ATI; PCIC; FPA
keywords: agencies; partners; government; DA attached agencies

title: Municipal agriculture office as first contact
content: Farmers usually coordinate first with their Municipal Agriculture Office (MAO) or City Agriculture Office. The MAO assists with farmer registration, technical advice, referral to DA-CAR programs, and pest or disease reports.
keywords: MAO; municipal agriculturist; LGU; farmer assistance

title: RSBSA farmer registration
content: The Registry System for Basic Sectors in Agriculture (RSBSA) is the DA database of farmers, farm workers, and fisherfolk. Being listed is commonly required to receive subsidies, inputs, and other DA assistance. Registration is done through the local MAO.
keywords: RSBSA; registration; farmer ID; subsidy eligibility

title: Highland vegetables of the Cordillera
content: Benguet and nearby areas supply a large share of the country's temperate (highland) vegetables, including cabbage, white potato, carrots, Chinese cabbage (wombok), broccoli, cauliflower, lettuce, sweet pea, and snap beans. The cool climate at higher elevations suits crops that do poorly in lowland heat.
keywords: highland vegetables; Benguet; cabbage; potato; carrots; cool climate

title: Cabbage production basics
content: Cabbage is usually raised from seedlings transplanted about 3 to 4 weeks after sowing. Use well-drained, loose soil with good organic matter and a pH of about 6.0 to 6.8. Practice crop rotation with non-cruciferous crops to reduce clubroot and other soil-borne diseases.
season: Dry season and early wet season
keywords: cabbage; transplanting; crop rotation; clubroot; soil pH

title: Potato: use clean seed
content: Using certified or disease-free seed tubers is one of the most effective ways to reduce disease in potato. Plant in well-drained soil, do hilling a few weeks after emergence, and avoid planting potato repeatedly in the same plot. Seed sources should be verified with DA-CAR or BPI.
keywords: potato; seed tubers; hilling; certified seed; crop rotation

title: Late blight in potato and tomato
content: Late blight is a fungal-like disease favored by cool, wet, and humid weather, common in highland areas. Signs include dark water-soaked leaf spots that spread quickly. Management includes resistant varieties, clean seed, good field drainage, field sanitation, and timely fungicide use following label directions and local technician advice.
keywords: late blight; potato; tomato; fungal disease; cool humid

title: Diamondback moth in crucifers
content: Diamondback moth is a major pest of cabbage and other crucifers, and it can develop resistance when the same insecticide is used repeatedly. Use integrated pest management (IPM): regular scouting, rotating chemical classes, using biological control where available, and removing crop residues after harvest.
keywords: diamondback moth; IPM; insecticide resistance; cabbage; pest scouting

title: Strawberry in La Trinidad
content: La Trinidad, Benguet is widely known as the strawberry capital of the Philippines. Strawberries are propagated through runners, grown on raised beds covered with mulch, and harvested when fruits are fully red. Fruits are delicate and should be sold or processed quickly.
season: Cool dry months are peak harvest
keywords: strawberry; La Trinidad; runners; mulch; raised beds

title: Arabica coffee in the Cordillera
content: Arabica coffee is well suited to the higher elevations of the Cordillera, generally grown at roughly 1,000 meters above sea level or higher. Shade trees, proper pruning, and selective picking of ripe red cherries help improve cup quality.
location_scope: Benguet; Mountain Province; Kalinga; Ifugao; Apayao
season: Harvest generally in the cooler months
keywords: Arabica; coffee; elevation; shade trees; selective picking

title: Basic coffee post-harvest handling
content: Pick only ripe cherries, process them soon after harvest, and dry the beans evenly on raised beds or clean drying platforms, turning them often. Dry beans should be stored in clean, ventilated, moisture-free conditions to avoid mold and off-flavors.
keywords: coffee; drying; storage; mold; post-harvest

title: Ifugao Rice Terraces and heirloom rice
content: The Ifugao Rice Terraces are a centuries-old agricultural heritage system, and the Cordillera is known for traditional heirloom rice varieties often grown once a year in terraced fields. Heirloom rice is valued for its cultural significance, aroma, and market potential as a specialty product.
keywords: heirloom rice; Ifugao; terraces; tinawon; cultural heritage

title: Rice transplanting guide
content: For transplanted rice, seedlings are usually moved to the field when they are about 18 to 25 days old, with common spacing around 20 cm x 20 cm. Level the field well, maintain proper water depth, and transplant one to three seedlings per hill depending on the variety and extension advice.
keywords: rice; transplanting; seedling age; spacing; land preparation

title: Alternate wetting and drying (AWD)
content: AWD is a water-saving practice where the field is allowed to dry for a short period before re-irrigating, rather than staying continuously flooded. Using a field water tube helps monitor the water level. It can reduce water use and methane emissions when applied correctly.
keywords: AWD; water saving; irrigation; methane; field water tube

title: RCEF for rice farmers
content: The Rice Competitiveness Enhancement Fund (RCEF) was created under the Rice Tariffication Law (Republic Act 11203). It supports rice farmers through certified seeds, farm machinery, credit, and extension and training. Eligibility and current program components should be confirmed with DA-CAR or the local MAO.
keywords: RCEF; Rice Tariffication Law; RA 11203; seeds; machinery

title: Golden apple snail control in rice
content: Golden apple snails damage young rice seedlings. Control options include proper land leveling, keeping water shallow in early crop stages, hand-picking snails and egg masses, and using screens at water inlets. Use only registered molluscicides following label instructions.
keywords: golden apple snail; rice; pest; egg masses; water management

title: Fall armyworm in corn
content: Fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) feeds on corn leaves and whorls and spreads quickly. Scout fields early, remove egg masses and larvae where possible, plant at the same time as neighboring farms to reduce build-up, and follow DA and BPI recommendations on control options.
keywords: fall armyworm; corn; scouting; IPM; pest

title: Root crops: sweet potato and ginger
content: Sweet potato, ginger, and other root crops are commonly grown in the Cordillera and are suited to sloping, well-drained land. Use healthy planting material, avoid waterlogged soil, and practice rotation to reduce disease build-up.
keywords: sweet potato; ginger; root crops; planting material; rotation

title: Contour farming on slopes
content: Much Cordillera farmland is on steep slopes where erosion is a serious risk. Planting along the contour, using grass or shrub strips, building terraces, and keeping soil covered with mulch or crops helps reduce soil loss and runoff.
season: Year-round, especially before the rainy season
keywords: erosion; contour farming; terraces; mulch; slopes

title: SALT for sloping lands
content: Sloping Agricultural Land Technology (SALT) combines hedgerows of nitrogen-fixing plants planted along contour lines with food crops grown in the alleys between them. This reduces erosion, improves soil fertility, and provides fodder or green manure.
agency: DA; Mindanao Baptist Rural Life Center (originator)
keywords: SALT; hedgerows; agroforestry; upland farming; soil fertility

title: Soil testing before fertilizing
content: A soil test shows pH, organic matter, and nutrient levels so fertilizer is applied according to actual needs rather than guesswork. Farmers can ask the Bureau of Soils and Water Management (BSWM) or the DA regional soils laboratory about sampling and testing procedures.
keywords: soil test; fertilizer; pH; BSWM; nutrient management

title: Making compost
content: Compost can be made from crop residues, vegetable trimmings, and animal manure by layering green (nitrogen-rich) and brown (carbon-rich) materials, keeping the pile moist but not soggy, and turning it periodically. Finished compost is dark, crumbly, and earthy-smelling, and it improves soil structure and water retention.
keywords: compost; organic fertilizer; green and brown materials; soil health

title: Organic agriculture in the Philippines
content: The Organic Agriculture Act of 2010 (Republic Act 10068) provides the legal framework for promoting organic farming. Organic producers should follow standards on soil management, avoidance of prohibited inputs, and record-keeping. Certification and program details should be confirmed with the DA Bureau of Agriculture and Fisheries Standards or the regional office.
keywords: organic agriculture; RA 10068; certification; standards

title: African swine fever (ASF) biosecurity
content: ASF is a highly contagious viral disease of pigs with no widely available cure. Key biosecurity steps: restrict visitors and vehicles, disinfect boots and equipment, avoid feeding swill, source pigs from known healthy farms, and immediately report sick or dead pigs to the local veterinarian or MAO.
keywords: ASF; swine; biosecurity; disease reporting; swill feeding

title: Native chicken raising
content: Native chickens are hardy and adapted to local conditions, and are often raised in free-range or semi-confined systems for household income. Provide clean water, a dry shelter against predators, supplemental feed, and vaccination as advised by the local veterinarian.
keywords: native chicken; free-range; vaccination; backyard poultry

title: Highly pathogenic avian influenza reporting
content: Sudden deaths in poultry, swollen heads, or drops in egg production may indicate avian influenza. Isolate affected birds, limit movement of people and equipment, and report immediately to the local veterinarian, MAO, or the DA regional animal health office.
keywords: avian influenza; bird flu; poultry; disease reporting; isolation

title: Freshwater fish in the highlands
content: Some highland communities raise freshwater species such as tilapia in suitable water conditions, and cold-water areas may support species like trout. Site selection, clean water supply, appropriate stocking density, and BFAR technical guidance are important before starting a fish farm.
season: Varies by species and water temperature
keywords: tilapia; trout; aquaculture; fish pond; BFAR

title: Benguet Agri-Pinoy Trading Center
content: The Benguet Agri-Pinoy Trading Center in La Trinidad is a trading hub where highland vegetables are brought, sorted, and sold to buyers from Metro Manila and other areas. Farmers should check current prices, grading requirements, and trading rules with the market administration.
keywords: trading post; La Trinidad; vegetable prices; grading; market

title: Reducing post-harvest losses in vegetables
content: Harvest during cooler parts of the day, handle produce gently, use clean ventilated crates instead of sacks, sort and grade before transport, and avoid overloading trucks. Better handling reduces bruising, rot, and price discounts.
keywords: post-harvest loss; crates; grading; cool chain; handling

title: Crop insurance with PCIC
content: The Philippine Crop Insurance Corporation (PCIC) offers insurance for crops, livestock, and other farm assets against losses due to natural calamities and certain pests and diseases. Registered farmers can ask the PCIC office or MAO about coverage, premiums, and subsidy availability.
season: Apply before or early in the cropping season
keywords: PCIC; crop insurance; typhoon; calamity; coverage

title: Accessing agricultural credit
content: Farmers can seek agricultural loans from government financial institutions such as the Land Bank of the Philippines and from cooperatives and rural banks, and may also inquire about credit programs supported by the Agricultural Credit Policy Council (ACPC). Requirements and interest rates vary, so confirm current terms before applying.
keywords: agricultural loan; ACPC; LandBank; cooperative; credit

title: Safe pesticide use
content: Use only pesticides registered with the Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority (FPA), read the label, wear protective equipment, observe the pre-harvest interval, and never reuse empty containers for food or water. Store chemicals locked and away from children and food.
keywords: pesticide safety; FPA; PPE; pre-harvest interval; label

title: Good Agricultural Practices (GAP)
content: Good Agricultural Practices are farm-level practices that promote food safety, environmental care, and worker welfare. They include safe water use, proper manure handling, hygiene, traceable record-keeping, and responsible input use. GAP certification can help farmers access better markets.
keywords: GAP; food safety; certification; record-keeping; traceability

title: Typhoon and rainy season preparedness
content: In the Cordillera, heavy rains and typhoons can cause landslides, flooding, and crop losses. Before the season, clean drainage canals, harvest mature crops early when a typhoon is forecast, secure stored inputs and livestock, and monitor PAGASA advisories and local DA announcements.
keywords: typhoon; landslide; drainage; PAGASA; disaster preparedness

title: Farmer field school
content: A Farmer Field School (FFS) is a season-long, hands-on learning approach where farmers meet regularly in the field to observe crops, test practices, and make group decisions on pest and nutrient management. FFS is commonly offered through DA and ATI programs in partnership with local governments.
keywords: farmer field school; ATI; training; IPM; group learning

title: Tagalog quick tip: pagtatanim sa tamang panahon
content: Mahalagang alamin ang tamang panahon ng pagtatanim sa inyong lugar. Magtanong sa Municipal Agriculture Office o DA-CAR tungkol sa cropping calendar, uri ng binhi, at lagay ng panahon para mabawasan ang pinsala sa pananim.
keywords: cropping calendar; tamang panahon; binhi; Tagalog; panahon
